question.problem:
The disjoint union ${A}_{1}⊔{A}_{2}⊔{A}_{3}$ of events ${A}_{1},{A}_{2},{A}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space. Compute $P({A}_{2}|B)$ given the following probabilities:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P(B|{A}_{1})=0.1, & P({A}_{1})=0.15 \\  & P(B|{A}_{2})=0.2, & P({A}_{2})=0.46 \\  & P(B|{A}_{3})=0.6, & P({A}_{3})=0.39\end{aligned}
$$

Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.

current_example.problem:
The disjoint union $A_1 \sqcup A_2 \sqcup A_3$ of events $A_1,A_2,A_3$ covers the entire sample space. Compute $P(A_1|B)$ given the following probabilities:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P(B|{A}_{1})=0.23, &  \\  & P(B|{A}_{2})=0.26, & P({A}_{2})=0.3 \\  & P(B|{A}_{3})=0.18, & P({A}_{3})=0.4\end{aligned}
$$
current_example.worked_solution:
If the disjoint union $A_1 \sqcup A_2 \sqcup \ldots \sqcup A_n$ covers the entire sample space, Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability gives us the following:

$$
P(A_k | B) = \dfrac{P(B|A_k) P(A_k)}{P(B)} = \dfrac{P(B|A_k) P(A_k)}{\sum_{i=1}^n P(B|A_i)P(A_i)}
$$

where $k=1,2,\ldots,n.$

In our case, $n=3,$ and $A_1 \sqcup A_2 \sqcup A_3$ covers the entire sample space. Consequently, we have

$$
P(A_1) + P(A_2) + P(A_3) = 1.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}P({A}_{1}) & =1-(P({A}_{2})+P({A}_{3})) \\  & =1-(0.3+0.4) \\  & =0.3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P({A}_{1}|B) & =\frac{P(B|{A}_{1})P({A}_{1})}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{3}P(B|{A}_{i})P({A}_{i})} \\  & =\frac{P(B|{A}_{1})P({A}_{1})}{P(B|{A}_{1})P({A}_{1})+P(B|{A}_{2})P({A}_{2})+P(B|{A}_{3})P({A}_{3})} \\  & =\frac{(0.23)(0.3)}{(0.23)(0.3)+(0.26)(0.3)+(0.18)(0.4)} \\  & =\frac{0.069}{0.219} \\  & ≈0.315.\end{aligned}
$$
